one_liner: C audio feature-extraction library (mel, MFCC, CQT, CWT, pitch) with Python bindings; mel spectrograms faster than librosa, mostly torchaudio-competitive.
what_it_does: audioFlux computes time-frequency transforms (STFT-style BFT, NSGT, CWT, CQT, VQT, ST, DWT/WPT/SWT, reassignment and synchrosqueezing) and spectral, cepstral, chroma, pitch, onset and HPSS features from a C core. The Python API is object-based (e.g. af.MelSpectrogram(num, samplate, radix2_exp, slide_length, ...).spectrogram(x)) and calls the shared library through ctypes; it is not a drop-in replacement for librosa's functional API, and FFT sizes are given as powers of two (radix2_exp). The C library can also be built for iOS, Android, Windows and OpenHarmony.
how_it_is_fast: Per-frame FFTs go to a vendor FFT chosen at build time: Intel MKL DFTI on Linux, Apple Accelerate vDSP on macOS/iOS, FFTW3f on Android/Windows, or a built-in cached-twiddle radix-2 FFT. The STFT splits frames across omp_get_max_threads()/2 OpenMP worker FFT objects (32 threads on the 64-thread Threadripper 3970X used for the headline chart). The mel filter bank is built once when the object is created and applied as a matrix product, so repeated calls only pay for FFT, power and the dot product.
when_to_use: Batch extraction of mel, MFCC, CQT or chroma features from long clips in Python on x86-64 Linux or macOS, where the C core's multi-threaded STFT pays off (500 to 3000 frames per call)
Replacing librosa.feature.melspectrogram in a data pipeline that calls it many times, since audioFlux builds the filter bank once and keeps it in the object
Mobile or embedded feature extraction from C (iOS Accelerate, Android FFTW3f builds) where pulling in PyTorch is not an option; the README reports 0.25 to 0.89 ms per 4096-sample mel frame on phones
Research that needs less common transforms (NSGT, S-transform, synchrosqueezed CWT, reassigned STFT) in one library
when_not_to_use: You already depend on PyTorch: torchaudio was as fast or faster on the Intel i7-6850K Linux box at 10 frames and above, at 100 frames on the Threadripper, and for short inputs on both Macs

You need outputs that match librosa or torchaudio numerically: the benchmark never compares outputs, defaults differ (Slaney scale without filter normalisation here), and open issue #35 reports different mel values when torch is imported in the same process
Linux ARM64 or other platforms without a prebuilt library: issue #44 (arm64 Docker) is unanswered, and the PyPI package is a single 70.8 MB py3-none-any wheel carrying prebuilt binaries

Very long inputs on memory-constrained devices: issue #27 reports 1.4 GB allocated for a 3-minute track (15 M samples, hop 512) on Android; the STFT stores full fftLength complex frames, not just the fftLength/2+1 non-redundant bins

Projects that need a responsive upstream: most issues since 2023 have no maintainer reply, including #46, an unreported vulnerability (the reporter could not file it because GitHub security reporting is off)

integration.form: shared lib (C core built with CMake) plus Python package (ctypes wrapper); static lib on iOS
integration.dependencies: Linux: optional Intel MKL (MKL_INCLUDE_PATH/MKL_LIB_PATH) and LLVM libomp; macOS: Accelerate and libomp (Homebrew llvm); Android/Windows/OHOS: FFTW3f; Python: numpy, scipy>=1.2.0, soundfile>=0.12.1, matplotlib
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.5; Linux CMakeLists hard-codes /usr/bin/clang with -O3 -fopenmp=libomp; macOS needs Homebrew llvm (C_COMPILER_PATH); Python >=3.6; setup.py refuses to build on Windows (cross-built from macOS/Linux)
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (x86-64, Apple M1), Windows, iOS, Android, OpenHarmony per the build scripts; Linux arm64 not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; objects cache per-call buffers internally, so use one object per thread; the STFT itself runs OpenMP threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same features as librosa and torchaudio but a different object API, power-of-two FFT sizes only, and different mel defaults, so outputs are not identical

gotchas: The STFT calls omp_set_num_threads() on each call (timeLength threads for short inputs, omp_get_max_threads()/2 otherwise), changing the OpenMP thread count other code in the same runtime then inherits; the benchmark README also warns that mixing its libomp with MKL/PyTorch OpenMP runtimes can fail or slow down
On Apple platforms the real-input FFT goes through the complex vDSP_fft_zop path because, per a source comment, 'real to complex fft has problem', so it does twice the FFT work there
The PyPI release is still 0.1.9 (2024-05-24); the TuneTrack features (README 'v0.1.10', commits of 2026-02/03) are only in the source tree
benchmark/run_benchmark.py treats -r as the number of subprocess launches and -er as calls per launch, the reverse of what benchmark/README.md says; the per-call average it prints is still correct
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling does audio feature extraction: pedalboard covers effects and file I/O against pySoX and librosa.load, and libsoxr/r8brain cover resampling, so pick audioFlux when the job is mel/MFCC/CQT features and you cannot or do not want to depend on PyTorch.
verified_claims_summary: First-party benchmark (audioFlux 0.1.5, librosa 0.10.0, torchaudio 0.11.0; 2048-point FFT, hop 512, 128 mels, average per call reported as seconds per 1000 calls) on a Threadripper 3970X, i7-6850K, macOS Intel i7 and Apple M1, with build flags, BLAS backend and thread counts not recorded: against torchaudio audioFlux is 1.2x to 7.1x faster on the 3970X except at 100 frames (0.92x), slower on the i7-6850K from 10 frames up, and faster on the Macs only for long inputs. The 10x to 56x librosa ratios overstate the core's advantage: run_librosa.py times librosa.feature.melspectrogram, which in librosa 0.10.0 rebuilds the 128-band mel filter bank on every call (filters.mel cache is off unless LIBROSA_CACHE_DIR is set) and is called without sr (22050 Hz default instead of 32000), while audioFlux's and torchaudio's filter banks are built at object creation outside the timer; audioFlux also runs up to 32 OpenMP threads with no thread limits set for any library.
status_note: MIT-licensed and usable from Python today, but maintenance is sporadic: no PyPI release since 0.1.9 (2024-05-24), a commit gap from May 2024 to February 2026, and most open issues (including an unreported vulnerability) without a maintainer reply.
